INTERNAL FLIGHT ALTERNATIVE

[11] I must consider a two-prong test in order to determine the viability of an IFA location. Firstly, I must be satisfied that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant would not face a serious possibility of persecution or risk to their life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the proposed IFA. Secondly, I must be satisfied that conditions in the suggested IFA are not such that it would be objectively unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, for her to relocate and reside there.

[12] Once the possibility of an IFA is raised, the burden shifts to the claimant to show, on a balance of probabilities, that there is a serious possibility of persecution, or a section 97(1) risk, in the IFA locations.7

argument_evidence.context_text: Generalized violence does not render an IFA location unsafe under the first prong of the IFA test.
I accept that people do get murdered in Roatan, but that does not render Roatan unsafe on the first prong of the IFA test.

subthemes.text:
[23] The National Documentation Package (NDP) for Honduras10 does not mention a presence of this gang or any other Honduran gang in Roatan, nor does it establish that the Barrio 18 have alliances with groups in Roatan which could assist it in locating the claimant.

[24] The claimant provided post-hearing documents which discuss murders of various persons in Roatan and the Bay Islands.11 None of these articles identify the culprits or the motivation for these murders.

[25] I am unaware of any locale anywhere on earth that can accurately claim to be entirely free of violence and Roatan is no exception. I accept that people do get murdered in Roatan, but that does not render Roatan unsafe on the first prong of the IFA test. Generalized violence does not render an IFA location unsafe under the first prong of the IFA test.

[26] One of the articles submitted12 discusses how a member of Barrio-18 allegedly worked for a 911 call center in the capital of Tegucigalpa and was discovered after receiving a call for assistance.

[27] The fact that members of the gang have infiltrated such services is not surprising, as corruption in Honduras is well discussed in the NDP. However, in my view the fact that the gang had a member in a 911 call center in the capital city does not establish on a balance of probabilities that they could locate the claimant in Roatan.

subthemes.text:
[28] I do not have evidence before me that this call center also services the island of Roatan for example, or that even if the gang knew the claimant was in Roatan, that they would have the means to actually locate her. General information about corruption elsewhere in Honduras does not assist me in determining whether the gang has the means (and what they are) to locate the claimant in Roatan.

[29] As such, I find that the claimant has not demonstrated on a balance of probabilities that Barrio 18 has the means and motivation to locate her in Roatan or elsewhere in Honduras. If the gang does not have the means and motivation to locate the claimant in the IFA location, then it cannot be said that the claimant faces a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or a s. 97(1) risk on a balance of probabilities.

[30] The second aspect of the IFA analysis requires me to consider all the circumstances specific to the claimant to determine if relocating to the proposed IFA location would be unreasonable. The second prong of the IFA test may be stated as follows: would it be unduly harsh to expect the claimant to move to another, less hostile part of the country before seeking refugee status abroad?

[31] The test is an objective one: is it objectively reasonable to expect the claimant to seek safety in a different part of the country? Thirunavukkarasu13 sets a very high threshold for what makes an IFA unreasonable in all the circumstances. The hardship associated with dislocation and relocation is not the kind of undue hardship that renders an IFA unreasonable. The standard is high and requires proof of adverse conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of the claimant in travelling to and in living in the IFA location.

[32] Moving on to the second prong of the test, I asked the claimant if safety aside, there was any other reason why she could not relocate to Roatan. She did not provide any other reasons specific to her circumstances that were not related to safety.

[33] Counsel submits that failed refugee claimants from Honduras who have returned to Tegucigalpa have in some cases been killed. This certainly makes sense because the capital is the main power base for the Barrio 18 and MS-13 gangs according to the NDP.

[34] If the claimant is faced with a return to Honduras, she can simply avoid returning to Tegucigalpa, however. If the claimant chooses to return to the exact same city where her problems began, then she is voluntarily subjecting herself to that risk.

[35] The claimant has the option to relocate to Roatan where she would not on a balance of probabilities face a s. 97(1) risk to life, if she chooses.

[36] I find therefore that the claimant has not demonstrated on a balance of probabilities that the proposed IFA location is unreasonable in considering all of her personal circumstances.

REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the claimant) is a citizen of Honduras and claims refugee protection pursuant to ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1
ALLEGATIONS

[2] The claimant's allegations are fully set out in her Basis of Claim (BOC) form.2 To summarize, the claimant alleges a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground and a risk to life and of cruel and unusual punishment or treatment in Honduras by the Barrio 18 criminal organization.
DETERMINATION

[3] I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee under s. 96, nor a person in need of protection under s. 97(1) of IRPA. She has failed to demonstrate a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or a risk to life or of cruel and unusual punishment or treatment on a balance of probabilities which exists throughout Honduras.
DETERMINATIVE ISSUES

[4] The determinative issue in this claim was the existence of a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Roatan.
ANALYSIS
Identity

[5] The claimant's personal identity as a national of Honduras is established on a balance of probabilities by her genuine Honduran passport3 and her U.S. biometrics4.
Credibility

[6] The claimant was a credible witness on a balance of probabilities. Her evidence was consistent with her narrative and was generally supported by documentary evidence and the country conditions documents.

[8] The Barrio 18 gang's interest in the claimant is criminal in nature. Her brother co-operated with police, resulting in the arrest and imprisonment of one of their members and they retaliated by murdering his son. They remain interested in locating the brother and are harassing his family members in an attempt to discern his whereabouts.
[9] Barrio 18 is a criminal gang. Threats are criminal acts and criminal acts do not generally form a nexus to the Convention.6

[10] I therefore find that the gang is targeting the claimant for criminal reasons and not reasons captured by one of the Convention grounds and therefore, this claim shall be assessed under s. 97(1).
INTERNAL FLIGHT ALTERNATIVE

[11] I must consider a two-prong test in order to determine the viability of an IFA location. Firstly, I must be satisfied that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant would not face a serious possibility of persecution or risk to their life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the proposed IFA. Secondly, I must be satisfied that conditions in the suggested IFA are not such that it would be objectively unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, for her to relocate and reside there.

[12] Once the possibility of an IFA is raised, the burden shifts to the claimant to show, on a balance of probabilities, that there is a serious possibility of persecution, or a section 97(1) risk, in the IFA locations.7

[13] I considered whether a viable Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) exists for the claimant in Roatan. Roatan is an island which is approximately 261 kilometres from Tegucigalpa and is only accessible by air or by water. The NDP for Honduras8 does not demonstrate a presence of the Barrio 18 in this location.

[14] In assessing whether the proposed IFA location is safe, I must consider whether the agent of harm in this case has both the means and motivation9 to pursue the claimant in the IFA location, should she return to Honduras.

[15] Regarding the motivation to locate the claimant, the claimant was unable to demonstrate that Barrio 18 has made any attempts to divine her location since she has been outside of the country. The claimant provided several letters from her spouse, children and other family members and none of them mention any attempts to locate her or ask about where she might be.

[16] The claimant testified that her nephew was approached by the Barrio 18 gang after she left Honduras, but her information was that this was related to their belief that he worked for police, when in reality, he just provided XXXX XXXX there. It does not appear that this incident has anything to do with the claimant.

[17] The claimant believes that the Barrio 18 would be motivated to locate her because they have yet to locate her brother and get their revenge. It does appear that the gang has a strong and persistent motivation to locate her brother, even though they have not located him in over a decade of trying.
[18] The motivation to locate the claimant does not appear to be as strong. Their interest in her is directly related to their desire to locate her brother.

[19] Given that the Barrio 18 stopped attending the church in 2018 after the claimant left and have not made attempts to locate her since 2018, I find that the claimant has not established on a balance of probabilities, that the gang has a strong motivation to locate her throughout Honduras.
[20] The second consideration for me is whether Barrio 18 have the means to locate the claimant in Roatan.

[21] As I mentioned above, the gang does not have a physical presence in Roatan. Counsel correctly submits that there is a distinction between having a physical presence in a location and being able to reach a target in that location.

[22] However, where an organization does not have a demonstrated physical presence in a particular location, the onus remains on the claimant to point to objective evidence that demonstrates how an agent of harm can reach someone in a location where they are not physically present.

[23] The National Documentation Package (NDP) for Honduras10 does not mention a presence of this gang or any other Honduran gang in Roatan, nor does it establish that the Barrio 18 have alliances with groups in Roatan which could assist it in locating the claimant.

[24] The claimant provided post-hearing documents which discuss murders of various persons in Roatan and the Bay Islands.11 None of these articles identify the culprits or the motivation for these murders.

[25] I am unaware of any locale anywhere on earth that can accurately claim to be entirely free of violence and Roatan is no exception. I accept that people do get murdered in Roatan, but that does not render Roatan unsafe on the first prong of the IFA test. Generalized violence does not render an IFA location unsafe under the first prong of the IFA test.
[26] One of the articles submitted12 discusses how a member of Barrio-18 allegedly worked for a 911 call center in the capital of Tegucigalpa and was discovered after receiving a call for assistance.

[27] The fact that members of the gang have infiltrated such services is not surprising, as corruption in Honduras is well discussed in the NDP. However, in my view the fact that the gang had a member in a 911 call center in the capital city does not establish on a balance of probabilities that they could locate the claimant in Roatan.

[28] I do not have evidence before me that this call center also services the island of Roatan for example, or that even if the gang knew the claimant was in Roatan, that they would have the means to actually locate her. General information about corruption elsewhere in Honduras does not assist me in determining whether the gang has the means (and what they are) to locate the claimant in Roatan.

[29] As such, I find that the claimant has not demonstrated on a balance of probabilities that Barrio 18 has the means and motivation to locate her in Roatan or elsewhere in Honduras. If the gang does not have the means and motivation to locate the claimant in the IFA location, then it cannot be said that the claimant faces a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or a s. 97(1) risk on a balance of probabilities.

[30] The second aspect of the IFA analysis requires me to consider all the circumstances specific to the claimant to determine if relocating to the proposed IFA location would be unreasonable. The second prong of the IFA test may be stated as follows: would it be unduly harsh to expect the claimant to move to another, less hostile part of the country before seeking refugee status abroad?

[31] The test is an objective one: is it objectively reasonable to expect the claimant to seek safety in a different part of the country? Thirunavukkarasu13 sets a very high threshold for what makes an IFA unreasonable in all the circumstances. The hardship associated with dislocation and relocation is not the kind of undue hardship that renders an IFA unreasonable. The standard is high and requires proof of adverse conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of the claimant in travelling to and in living in the IFA location.

[32] Moving on to the second prong of the test, I asked the claimant if safety aside, there was any other reason why she could not relocate to Roatan. She did not provide any other reasons specific to her circumstances that were not related to safety.

[33] Counsel submits that failed refugee claimants from Honduras who have returned to Tegucigalpa have in some cases been killed. This certainly makes sense because the capital is the main power base for the Barrio 18 and MS-13 gangs according to the NDP.

[34] If the claimant is faced with a return to Honduras, she can simply avoid returning to Tegucigalpa, however. If the claimant chooses to return to the exact same city where her problems began, then she is voluntarily subjecting herself to that risk.
[35] The claimant has the option to relocate to Roatan where she would not on a balance of probabilities face a s. 97(1) risk to life, if she chooses.
[36] I find therefore that the claimant has not demonstrated on a balance of probabilities that the proposed IFA location is unreasonable in considering all of her personal circumstances.

[37] Roatan is therefore a viable internal flight alternative for the claimant, which is both safe and reasonable for her, given her personal circumstances.
CONCLUSION

[38] I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. She has failed to demonstrate a serious possibility of persecution or a risk to life or of cruel and unusual punishment or treatment on a balance of probabilities which exists throughout Honduras.
[39] The claimant has a viable internal flight alternative in Roatan.

[40] Her claim is therefore rejected.
